what_its_for: Bupivacaine is a local anesthetic (numbing medicine) used to block pain in a specific area of your body. It is commonly used before or after surgery, during dental procedures, during childbirth (like an epidural), or for nerve block procedures to control pain. It works by temporarily stopping nerve signals so you do not feel pain in the treated area.
how_to_take: Bupivacaine is NOT a medicine you take by mouth at home. It is always given by a trained healthcare provider such as a doctor, nurse anesthetist, or anesthesiologist. It may be injected into a specific area of your body, given as an epidural (injection into the space around your spinal cord), or placed near nerves or surgical sites. You will receive this medicine in a clinic, hospital, or surgical center. Do not attempt to give this medicine to yourself or others.
dosing: Your dose will be decided entirely by your healthcare provider based on your age, weight, the procedure you are having, and the area being numbed. There is no standard home dosing. The medicine may start working within a few minutes and its numbing effect can last anywhere from a few hours up to 72 hours depending on the form used (for example, Exparel is a longer-acting form). Always follow the specific instructions given to you by your care team.
missed_dose: Because bupivacaine is given by a healthcare provider during a procedure or hospital stay and not taken on a regular schedule at home, the concept of a missed dose does not apply. If you have concerns about your pain management after a procedure, contact your healthcare provider or care team right away.
storage: You will not typically store this medicine at home. If for any reason a healthcare provider has given you special instructions for storage (for example, in a home care setting), keep it at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C), away from light, heat, and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not freeze it. Do not use it if the solution looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it.
what_to_avoid: While the numbed area has not fully recovered, avoid touching, rubbing, or applying heat (such as heating pads) to the numb area because you could injure yourself without realizing it. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or make important decisions until the numbness has completely worn off and you feel fully back to normal. Avoid alcohol after the procedure unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, especially other local anesthetics or heart medicines, as they can interact with bupivacaine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help immediately if you experience any of the following after receiving bupivacaine: seizures or convulsions, dizziness or fainting, irregular or fast heartbeat, chest pain or tightness, difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, severe swelling or redness at the injection site, numbness or weakness that lasts much longer than expected or spreads beyond the treated area, confusion or difficulty speaking, blurred vision, ringing in your ears, a metallic taste in your mouth, or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble swallowing. These could be signs of a serious reaction that needs immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Bupivacaine usually begins to numb the area within 5 to 30 minutes after it is given, depending on where it is injected and how much is used. The numbing effect typically lasts between 2 to 8 hours for standard forms of bupivacaine. The longer-acting form (Exparel) can provide pain relief for up to 72 hours (3 days). Your healthcare provider will tell you what to expect for your specific situation.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): Older patients may be more sensitive to the effects of bupivacaine and may need a lower dose. Pregnant women: Bupivacaine is commonly and safely used for epidurals during labor and delivery, but the type and dose will be carefully chosen by your care team. Children: It can be used in children but the dose must be carefully calculated based on weight; it is used with great caution in very young infants. People with liver problems: The liver breaks down bupivacaine, so those with liver disease may be at higher risk for side effects and will be monitored closely. People with heart conditions: Use extra caution is needed; tell your provider about any heart problems before receiving this medicine.
